t: Scipione del Ferro solves depressed cubic equations
c: 1520—Scipione del Ferro develops a method for solving "depressed" cubic equations (cubic equations without an x² term), but does not publish.

t: Adam Ries explains advantages of Arabic digits
c: 1522—Adam Ries explained the use of Arabic digits and their advantages over Roman numerals.

t: Nicolo Tartaglia solves depressed cubic equations
c: 1535—Nicolo Tartaglia independently develops a method for solving depressed cubic equations but also does not publish.

t: Gerolamo Cardano creates method for solving all cubics
c: 1539—Gerolamo Cardano learns Tartaglia's method for solving depressed cubics and discovers a method for depressing cubics, thereby creating a method for…

t: Lodovico Ferrari solves the quartic equation
c: 1540—Lodovico Ferrari solves the quartic equation.
1544—Michael Stifel publishes Arithmetica integra.
1545—Gerolamo Cardano conceives the idea of complex numbers.

t: Jyeṣṭhadeva writes Yuktibhāṣā with trigonometric proofs
c: 1550—Jyeṣṭhadeva, a Kerala school mathematician writes the Yuktibhāṣā, which gives proofs of power series expansion of some trigonometry functions.

t: Rafael Bombelli uses imaginary numbers for cubic equations
c: 1572—Rafael Bombelli writes the Algebra treatise and uses imaginary numbers to solve cubic equations.

t: Ludolph van Ceulen computes π to twenty places
c: 1596—Ludolph van Ceulen computes π to twenty decimal places using inscribed and circumscribed polygons.

t: John Napier publishes Napierian logarithm tables
c: 1614—John Napier publishes a table of Napierian logarithms in Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio.
1617—Henry Briggs discusses decimal logarithms in Logarithmorum Chilias Prima.

t: John Napier publishes first references to e
c: 1618—John Napier publishes the first references to e in a work on logarithms.
1619—Johannes Kepler discovers two of the Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra.

t: Pierre de Fermat develops rudimentary differential calculus
c: 1629—Pierre de Fermat develops a rudimentary differential calculus.

t: Gilles de Roberval proves cycloid area theorem
c: 1634—Gilles de Roberval shows that the area under a cycloid is three times the area of its generating circle.

t: Muhammad Baqir Yazdi discovers amicable numbers
c: 1636—Muhammad Baqir Yazdi jointly discovered the pair of amicable numbers 9,363,584 and 9,437,056 along with Descartes (1636).

t: Pierre de Fermat circulates analytic geometry manuscript
c: 1636—Pierre de Fermat circulates manuscript Methodus ad disquirendam maximam et minimam et de tangentibus linearum curvarum, a rudimentary differential…

t: René Descartes coins term imaginary number
c: 1637—First use of the term "imaginary number" by René Descartes; it was meant to be derogatory.

t: Pierre de Fermat claims proof of Last Theorem
c: 1637—Pierre de Fermat claims to have proven Fermat's Last Theorem in his copy of Diophantus' Arithmetica.
1637—René Descartes publishes La Géométrie containing his version of Analytic geometry
1643—René Descartes develops Descartes' theorem.

t: Pascal and Fermat create probability theory
c: 1654—Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat create the theory of probability.
1655—John Wallis writes Arithmetica Infinitorum.

t: Christopher Wren proves cycloid length theorem
c: 1658—Christopher Wren shows that the length of a cycloid is four times the diameter of its generating circle.
1665—Isaac Newton works on the fundamental theorem of calculus and develops his version of infinitesimal calculus.

t: Mercator and Brouncker discover logarithm series
c: 1668—Nicholas Mercator and William Brouncker discover an infinite series for the logarithm while attempting to calculate the area under a hyperbolic segment.
1671—James Gregory develops a series expansion for the inverse-tangent function (originally discovered by Madhava).
1673—Gottfried Leibniz also develops his version of infinitesimal calculus.

t: Isaac Newton invents functional root algorithm
c: 1675—Isaac Newton invents an algorithm for the computation of functional roots.

t: Gottfried Leibniz works on symbolic logic
c: 1680s – Gottfried Leibniz works on symbolic logic.
1683—Seki Takakazu develops elimination theory.

t: Leibniz discovers separation of variables technique
c: 1691—Gottfried Leibniz discovers the technique of separation of variables for ordinary differential equations.

t: Halley creates first statistical mortality tables
c: 1693—Edmund Halley prepares the first mortality tables statistically relating death rate to age.

t: L'Hôpital states rule for limit computation
c: 1696—Guillaume de l'Hôpital states his rule for the computation of certain limits.
1696—Jakob Bernoulli and Johann Bernoulli solve the brachistochrone problem, the first result in the calculus of variations.
1699—Abraham Sharp calculates π to 72 digits, but only 71 are correct.

t: Machin develops inverse-tangent series for π
c: 1706—John Machin develops a quickly converging inverse-tangent series for π and computes π to 100 decimal places.
1708—Seki Takakazu discovers Bernoulli numbers.
1712—Brook Taylor develops the Taylor series.

t: De Moivre states formula for complex numbers
c: 1722—Abraham de Moivre states de Moivre's formula connecting trigonometric functions and complex numbers.
1722—Takebe Kenko introduces Richardson extrapolation.

t: De Moivre founds theory of annuities
c: 1724—Abraham De Moivre studies mortality statistics and the foundation of the theory of annuities in Annuities on Lives.
1730—James Stirling publishes The Differential Method.
1733—Abraham de Moivre introduces the normal distribution to approximate the binomial distribution in probability.
1733—Giovanni Gerolamo Saccheri studies what geometry would be like if Euclid's fifth postulate were false.
1734—Leonhard Euler introduces the integrating factor technique for solving first-order ordinary differential equations.
1735—Leonhard Euler solves the Basel problem, relating an infinite series to π.

t: Euler solves homogeneous linear differential equations
c: 1739—Leonhard Euler solves the general homogeneous linear ordinary differential equation with constant coefficients.
1742—Christian Goldbach conjectures that every even number greater than two can be expressed as the sum of two primes, now known as Goldbach's conjecture.
1747—Jean le Rond d'Alembert solves the vibrating string problem (one-dimensional wave equation).
1748—Maria Gaetana Agnesi discusses analysis in Instituzioni Analitiche ad Uso della Gioventu Italiana.
1761—Johann Heinrich Lambert proves that π is irrational.
1762—Joseph-Louis Lagrange discovers the divergence theorem.

t: Vega computes π to 140 decimal places
c: 1789—Jurij Vega improves Machin's formula and computes π to 140 decimal places, 136 of which were correct.
1794—Jurij Vega publishes Thesaurus Logarithmorum Completus.
1796—Adrien-Marie Legendre conjectures the prime number theorem.
1796—Carl Friedrich Gauss proves that the regular 17-gon can be constructed using only a compass and straightedge.

t: Wessel links vectors with complex numbers
c: 1797—Caspar Wessel associates vectors with complex numbers and studies complex number operations in geometrical terms.

t: Gauss proves fundamental theorem of algebra
c: 1799—Carl Friedrich Gauss proves the fundamental theorem of algebra (every polynomial equation has a solution among the complex numbers).
1799—Paolo Ruffini partially proves the Abel–Ruffini theorem that quintic or higher equations cannot be solved by a general formula.
1801—Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, Carl Friedrich Gauss's number theory treatise, is published in Latin.

t: Legendre introduces method of least squares
c: 1805—Adrien-Marie Legendre introduces the method of least squares for fitting a curve to a given set of observations.

t: Argand proves fundamental theorem of algebra
c: 1806—Jean-Robert Argand publishes proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra and the Argand diagram.
1806—Louis Poinsot discovers the two remaining Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra.
1807—Joseph Fourier announces his discoveries about the trigonometric decomposition of functions.

t: Gauss examines complex integrals and path dependence
c: 1811—Carl Friedrich Gauss discusses the meaning of integrals with complex limits and briefly examines the dependence of such integrals on the chosen path of…

t: Poisson performs complex plane path integrations
c: 1815—Siméon Denis Poisson carries out integrations along paths in the complex plane.

t: Bolzano presents intermediate value theorem formally
c: 1817—Bernard Bolzano presents the intermediate value theorem—a continuous function that is negative at one point and positive at another point must be zero for…
1821—Augustin-Louis Cauchy publishes Cours d'Analyse, which purportedly contains an erroneous “proof” that the pointwise limit of continuous functions is…

t: Cauchy presents integral theorem for rectangles
c: 1822—Augustin-Louis Cauchy presents Cauchy's integral theorem for integration around the boundary of a rectangle in the complex plane.
1822—Irisawa Shintarō Hiroatsu analyzes Soddy's hexlet in a Sangaku.
1823 – Sophie Germain's Theorem is published in the second edition of Adrien-Marie Legendre's Essai sur la théorie des nombres
1824 – Niels Henrik Abel partially proves the Abel–Ruffini theorem that the general quintic or higher equations cannot be solved by a general formula involving…
1825 – André-Marie Ampère discovers Stokes' theorem.

t: Cauchy develops residue theory in complex analysis
c: 1825 – Augustin-Louis Cauchy presents the Cauchy integral theorem for general integration paths—he assumes the function being integrated has a continuous…

t: Dirichlet and Legendre prove Fermat's Last Theorem for n=5
c: 1825 – Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet and Adrien-Marie Legendre prove Fermat's Last Theorem for n = 5.

t: Abel refutes Cauchy's limit theorem claim
c: 1826 – Niels Henrik Abel gives counterexamples to Augustin-Louis Cauchy’s purported “proof” that the pointwise limit of continuous functions is continuous.
1829 – János Bolyai, Gauss, and Lobachevsky invent hyperbolic non-Euclidean geometry.
1831 – Mikhail Vasilievich Ostrogradsky rediscovers and gives the first proof of the divergence theorem earlier described by Lagrange, Gauss, and Green.

t: Galois founds group theory and Galois theory
c: 1832 – Évariste Galois presents a general condition for the solvability of algebraic equations, thereby essentially founding group theory and Galois theory.

t: Dirichlet proves Fermat's Last Theorem for n=14
c: 1832 – Lejeune Dirichlet proves Fermat's Last Theorem for n = 14.

t: Dirichlet proves theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions
c: 1835 – Lejeune Dirichlet proves Dirichlet's theorem about prime numbers in arithmetical progressions.
1837 – Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet develops analytic number theory.

t: Wantzel proves compass and straightedge impossibilities
c: 1837 – Pierre Wantzel proves that doubling the cube and trisecting the angle are impossible with only a compass and straightedge, as well as the full…
1838 – First mention of uniform convergence in a paper by Christoph Gudermann; later formalized by Karl Weierstrass.
1841 – Karl Weierstrass discovers but does not publish the Laurent expansion theorem.
1843 – Pierre-Alphonse Laurent discovers and presents the Laurent expansion theorem.
1843 – William Hamilton discovers the calculus of quaternions and deduces that they are non-commutative.
1844 - Hermann Grassmann publishes his Ausdehnungslehre, from which linear algebra is later developed.
1847 – George Boole formalizes symbolic logic in The Mathematical Analysis of Logic, defining what is now called Boolean algebra.
Drawing on Joule's experiments and other reasoning, Hermann Helmholtz set out the Principle of Conservation of Energy in 1847.

t: Stokes shows solitary waves from periodic combinations
c: 1849 – George Gabriel Stokes shows that solitary waves can arise from a combination of periodic waves.

t: Stokes rediscovers and proves Stokes' theorem
c: 1850 – George Gabriel Stokes rediscovers and proves Stokes' theorem.

t: Puiseux distinguishes poles and branch points
c: 1850 – Victor Alexandre Puiseux distinguishes between poles and branch points and introduces the concept of essential singular points.

t: Cayley uses quaternions to represent rotations
c: 1854 – Arthur Cayley shows that quaternions can be used to represent rotations in four-dimensional space.
